To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

family history is a strong predictor of cancer risk, and that the risk of cancer is influenced not only by the family history at a specific site, but also by family history at other sites, and that these associations are not limited to cancers of the same histology.
the familial aggregation of cancer is observed at multiple sites, and is not limited to recognized hereditary cancer syndromes.

family history of cancer is associated with the risk of developing cancer at the same site and at a number of other cancer sites, and that the associations between family history of cancer and cancer at other sites are stronger than those between family history of a cancer and the risk of the same cancer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of genetic variants associated with cancer susceptibility and with the study of their interactions with lifestyle and environmental exposures.
identifying and characterizing genetic and environmental factors that may influence the risk of cancer at different sites, with a view to developing prevention and early detection strategies.

the identification of the genetic factors that contribute to the development of cancer, with the aim of developing strategies for early detection, prevention and treatment of cancer, and for the improvement of the quality of life of cancer patients and survivors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the genetic factors that influence cancer risk are complex and multifactorial.
, in general, familial aggregations of cancers at several sites are more often due to shared exposures than to shared genetic factors, and the latter are likely to be of importance in only few cases.
the genetic contribution to familial aggregation of cancers is still poorly understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of developing a cancer is influenced by the presence of cancer at other sites within a family, and that the pattern of risk is not uniform across all sites.
the risk of cancer in relatives of cancer patients depends on the cancer site, the type of cancer, and the age of the patient at diagnosis.

, in addition to well-known familial cancer syndromes, there are a number of familial aggregations of cancers that are likely to be due to the presence of shared environmental exposures, but some are likely to have a genetic basis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
family history of cancer is a strong risk factor for several cancer sites.

the study of cancer family history is a promising approach for the identification of genes predisposing to multiple cancer types, and for the identification of cancer susceptibility genes that are involved in the etiology of several cancers.
family history can be used as an indicator of genetic susceptibility to a number of cancers.
